mainText:
If you only remember one thing today: the A I debate has flipped. U S tech giants are asking for rules, while Europe is easing off them.

Number one. Meta's open A I model.

From your Rundown newsletter: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an open weight model with eight hundred sixteen billion parameters, built for coding and agents. It worked with Apple, so two Mac Studios can run it locally, without the cloud. Meta calls it the most capable open weight model from the U S. But Chinese models like GLM, Kimi, and Qwen still score higher, especially at coding. It is the third big Western open release this month.

Why it matters: America is back in the open model race, but China still leads it.

Number two. Europe's A I identity crisis.

From your Politico Decoded newsletter, reporting from the International A I Summit in Dublin. European officials insist no new A I rules are needed. E U justice chief Michael McGrath said, quote, we are satisfied for now. Meanwhile, Microsoft's Brad Smith said the E U's A I Act may need a revamp, and called the U K's A I Security Institute the leader on evaluating A I. Demis Hassabis warned about autonomous A I agents, and said laws written three years ago may be out of date. A Siemens executive noted U S firms invested two hundred eighty billion dollars last year, versus twenty billion in Europe. Mistral's chief, Arthur Mensch, called leaving frontier models to America and China a fundamental mistake.

Why it matters: Europe built its reputation on regulation, and now it risks losing both the rule book and the race.

Number three. The White House Super Intelligence Force.

Also from Politico: the group's first meeting was held Thursday. It handed out assignments. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and cyber director Sean Cairncross will lead a group to monitor the companies' voluntary accord. The Pentagon's Emil Michael will build a process for labs to report breaches by their A I agents. The F T C will look at applying existing laws to A I. And the Labor Department will track job losses. Also today, Senate staff are getting access to Anthropic's Claude.

Why it matters: a voluntary pledge is starting to look like something with real oversight.

Number four. The A I money wobble.

Politico also reports tech stocks sold off. Markets now see a higher chance that data center firm CoreWeave defaults on its debt. Investors want proof the industry can survive rising interest rates and hardware costs. On the campaign side, Elon Musk has given at least two hundred seventy six million dollars in three months, making him the biggest spender of the midterms. Pro A I super packs, though, reported no new donations.

Why it matters: the technology is advancing, but the financing and the politics are getting shaky.

Number five. A I safety, security, and the gender gap.

Quick hits from your Rundown. Anthropic is giving six researchers from the group M E T R employee level access to assess its safety practices, and they can publish findings without approval. Bank of America hired a thousand contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos and other models. Open A I is training staff to spot espionage, including honeypot schemes. Amazon launched two A I wearables from seventy five dollars, and they work with Alexa.

Also in the Rundown: a Harvard study found that sixty four percent of working women got no A I training, versus forty nine percent of men. And A I headlines named men fourteen times as often as women.

Why it matters: the real A I divide is training, confidence, and who gets heard.

Also in your Reads. Tech Policy Press is launching a dialogue series on community built futures. And your Rundown shares a Friday habit: a scheduled Claude task that audits a company's workflow before the CEO wakes up.

Good news to close. Independent researchers are getting inside access to a top A I lab, and anyone with two Macs can now run a serious model privately. Safety checks and open tools are both moving forward.

The thread today: the people building A I are the ones asking for guardrails, and everyone is asking who pays for it. Have a great Friday, Sin.
